headline: Neutral as Waitsia asset ramp-up continues to disappoint despite valuation support
reasoning: Beach Energy's key Waitsia asset has faced persistent production ramp-up issues and the company recently downgraded production guidance. The free cash flow profile from FY28 looks attractive if Waitsia reaches nameplate capacity, but execution has consistently disappointed even Riesz's own expectations. He sees valuation support at current levels but recommends sticking with the major oil and gas names for pure oil price leverage.
quote: From a fundamental perspective, look, let's put aside the dividend yield for the time being... More importantly, or equally importantly, it will also bounce around with obviously the ramp up of one of the key assets. I think it's a wet seal. And that is still, it's ramping up, but it's still having problems. They just recently downgraded, or in the last year, they certainly downgraded production guidance. And at the end of the day, that is the key valuation driver over the next few years... this is a stock that has disappointed materially, even our expectations. And so, look, any time it gets below... $1 was always a good buy. But I mean, from an operational execution point of view, it continues to disappoint. So, I'm a neutral on this because I reckon there is valuation support, but the execution is little to desire.

headline: Riesz neutral on CSL as recent momentum-to-value rotation flatters the stock but margin recovery remains long-dated
reasoning: CSL has rallied 28% in one month driven by a broad rotation from high-momentum into low-momentum stocks rather than any fundamental improvement. Riesz still holds reservations about CSL's margin recovery in the core Behring business. Multiples of 25-30x were never warranted when earnings were under pressure, and these have now compressed to levels in line with peers at 12-14x. He sees a possible dividend-mandate argument at current prices but the fundamental turnaround is still distant.
quote: I just recently saw it. You're seeing a rotation back out from momentum stocks into low momentum stocks. And that's obviously healthcare. And so this is not just in Australia, but it's also globally. And it's the last couple of weeks and a half or two weeks. So you've seen CSL up 28% over a one-month period. I don't think fundamentally or from an earnings perspective, nothing's particularly changed for CSL. And we still hold reservations around CSLs, you know, sort of the margin recovery, the core bearing business... I think that kind of fizzes out a little bit when we start to get earnings update. And I think the turnaround in the earnings and the margins is still very much long dated, which is why CSL sold off in the first place.

headline: Riesz holds Evolution Mining as a preferred ASX gold exposure alongside Northern Star
reasoning: Evolution Mining is one of the two primary gold exposures in Riesz's portfolio, preferred over mid-tier producers like Genesis Minerals. The firm's long-term positive view on gold drives this positioning.
quote: We've been more exposed to Northern Star and Evolution Mining. But for me, it's a neutral [on GMD]. It's among that cohort of Gold stocks that you'd look to when gaining that exposure.

headline: Riesz holds Genesis Minerals as a quality mid-tier gold exposure but prefers Northern Star and Evolution Mining
reasoning: Riesz is broadly positive on gold long-term and sees merit in corporate activity within the sector, including Genesis's acquisition of Vault from Regis. The stock has gone sideways since March in line with the gold price. Genesis is on the watch list but the firm has more direct exposure through Northern Star and Evolution Mining, making Genesis a hold within the gold cohort rather than a top pick.
quote: I think the whole Gold space, even Gold today, was sold off because the hostilities in Iran have kicked off again. But I think we're still long-term positive on Gold. And so the equities that are leveraged to that will do well. Similar to Genesis, I think you'll see more and more corporate activity within this space, especially when it's sometimes, a lot of times, makes a lot more sense to acquire or merge to get that scale benefits and then divest underperforming assets rather than organically take particular assets through exploration to production. So overall, I think GMD is quite liked by the market. Obviously, since March has gone sideways, that's largely affecting what Gold has done to Xi. But to have a good rally, look, this is a stock that we've had on the watch list. We've been more exposed to Northern Star and Evolution Mining. But for me, it's a neutral.

headline: Riesz holds Goodman Group as quality data-centre-exposed industrial REIT with strong balance sheet; prefers it over Next DC
reasoning: Goodman Group's work-in-hand pipeline is now predominantly data center related, and the business offers high single-digit to low double-digit earnings growth with a strong balance sheet providing downside protection via its industrial property base. Riesz prefers Goodman over Next DC for data center exposure given the latter's high leverage. He notes that Australian property ETFs with large Goodman weightings are effectively AI thematic products, not pure REITs, and flags that global REITs have significantly outperformed Australian property year-to-date.
quote: I think Goodman Group is a good exposure versus something like, I think the next stock that we're going to discuss. So strong balance sheet gets you the work in hand report is all data center related now. And obviously it's still, and I think it will deliver that low, high single digit, low double digit earnings growth. And you get exposure to hopefully a more balanced exposure to data center thematic, because if something happens there or there's a moderation there, obviously there's the industrial space and a strong balance sheet to back it. So for us, I think the thematic and the quality of the business is well understood... Goodman Group for us is a hold and it's part of a quality portfolio.

headline: Riesz holds Macquarie Group as a core quality holding but would not chase at current levels; would back the truck up at $230
reasoning: Macquarie is a core holding in Riesz's portfolio where the firm is equal weight or slightly underweight the major banks but more positive on Macquarie. The recent rally followed a solid full-year result. The conglomerate structure blends annuity-style businesses with volatile market-facing ones (commodities delivered $1.5B one year and $4B in FY26) but generally provides a smooth ride through the cycle. He would not chase here but would add aggressively at $230.
quote: I totally agree with David. I think the recent rally, obviously on the back of the fully results, I think it was, and just the banking sector results in general were pretty acceptable to the market. So yeah, I wouldn't be chasing this. We own it in our portfolio as one of our core holdings with the banks. I think we're pretty much equal weight or slightly underweight banks, the four majors, and this is where we are a bit more positive. But the good thing, look, it's a good thing. It's a bad thing as well about Macquarie. It's got a bunch of businesses... as a conglomerate, it works, and it generally gives you a fairly smooth ride through the cycle. So it's a company that we're happy to hold. But, you know, I wouldn't be chasing any.

headline: Riesz prefers Northern Star as primary ASX gold exposure over mid-tier peers
reasoning: Riesz's firm has been more exposed to Northern Star and Evolution Mining as the preferred vehicles for gold price leverage, viewing them as better alternatives to mid-tier names like Genesis Minerals. The firm is long-term positive on gold and Northern Star provides scale and operational track record.
quote: We've been more exposed to Northern Star and Evolution Mining. But for me, it's a neutral [on GMD]. It's among that cohort of Gold stocks that you'd look to when gaining that exposure.

headline: Riesz has materially reduced Next DC exposure citing high leverage and overbuild risk if data centre demand moderates
reasoning: Riesz's firm has pulled back exposure to Next DC materially. The stock has strong market position as a pure-play data centre operator but carries high debt and is not expected to generate positive EPS for another four to five years. High capital intensity means the balance sheet cannot be easily adjusted if demand moderates, and historical parallels with US shale and regional data centre overbuilds suggest the sector faces meaningful default risk in a demand slowdown. With Goodman Group available as a better-balanced alternative with a superior balance sheet, owning both is redundant.
quote: We've pulled back our exposure to Next DC materially. It's the pure play. So if you want a pure play, yeah, Next DC. It does have strong market positions and whatnot. But again, the issue around the debt levels which you've just highlighted, no positive EPS expected for another four or five years... the issue around that Next DC is I think any moderation, when you've got high debt levels, any moderation in demand, which can happen, you're looking at very capital intensive businesses, which you cannot just switch on and off from a balance sheet perspective... data centers is one area we feel like where the perfect storm potentially shows up, which is high leverage, caught when demand moderates... why would you have both Next DC and Goodman Group in your portfolio when they effectively give you the same exposure? Why not just go Goodman Group, which has a better balance sheet?

headline: Riesz neutral on Treasury Wine Estates citing structural alcohol consumption decline and high execution risk on turnaround
reasoning: Treasury Wine Estates is attempting a complex turnaround under a new CEO involving brand rationalisation, US distribution overhaul and $100M in cost-outs, all while supporting margins through a portfolio rejig. Structural headwinds from lower alcohol consumption compound the bottom-up execution risk. Riesz's firm previously owned the stock but has exited. He would not allocate to it over better opportunities in a concentrated portfolio.
quote: I think most at Treasury Wine's recent investor day, just showed that these guys are trying to turn around a struggling ship. They're trying to, and look, the strategic direction of this turnaround strategy makes a lot of sense. But obviously, execution risk will be top of mind for investors. You're looking at reducing the number of brands that they're taking on board, or divesting some brands and focusing on a few high-quality brands... I think when you put potential structural elements at play, which is a lower consumption of alcohol, plus the bottom-up turnaround in terms of the strategic direction and the number of changes they're making to their operating model as well, it's a hard one. We exited the businesses. It's a hard one to get any more positive than a neutral.

headline: Riesz neutral on Viva Energy citing near-5x net debt/EBITDA and highly volatile refining earnings; prefers Ampol
reasoning: Viva Energy carries net debt of nearly 5x EBITDA, which is a significant balance sheet risk given that a material portion of earnings comes from refining — a highly volatile segment that delivered near-zero earnings in FY24 and FY25 before an expected $450-550M in FY26. The retail fuels business is more stable but insufficient to offset the risk profile. Riesz prefers Ampol in this space.
quote: It's got a net debt of EBITDA of nearly five times. That's a balance sheet, that risk that you just do not want to take when a significant part of your earnings, FI26 earnings, and even FI27 earnings are coming from refining. That can be a very, very volatile part of a business. You're looking at FI24, Viva got next to nothing, FI25, they got next to nothing, and now they're expected to deliver between $450 to $550 in refining. That's the kind of delta you're looking at. There's obviously the retail fuels marketing business is a lot more stable. For us, high debt levels, news to me that they're moving into Latin America. I actually don't think that that is necessarily correct. Apologies. All good. For us, the volatility in the refining earnings and then also the debt level is a concern. We prefer AMPOL in this space.

headline: Riesz bullish on global REITs which have been the best performing asset class year-to-date via a simple ETF
reasoning: Riesz identified global REITs as good value earlier in the year following research conducted during overseas travel. Year-to-date, global REITs accessed via a simple ETF (such as VanEck's product) have been the best performing asset class after infrastructure, outperforming all other categories. By contrast, the Vanguard Australian Property ETF (VAP) is down approximately 7% year-to-date, illustrating the benefit of diversifying into global property over Australian.
quote: One thing that we've been really positive on since the start of the sheet, which we picked up in our travels overseas was global REITs were looking really good value. But you had to go global REITs where there are a lot more sectors that you get exposure through, whether it's fund manager or ETF. And if you look at year-to-date returns, global REITs through a simple ETF like the VanEck one is the best performing just after infrastructure and as outperform all asset classes. Whereas VAF or VAP, I think it is the Vanguard Australian Properties ETF is down minus 7%.

headline: Riesz neutral on Karoon Energy pending production ramp-up to nameplate capacity, flags single-asset and jurisdiction risks
reasoning: Riesz is cautious on Karoon given it is a single-asset, pure-play producer still in ramp-up phase at its sole Brazilian asset. The recent Brazilian export tax extension highlights jurisdiction risk that will likely sustain a valuation discount. Free cash flow looks attractive from FY28 but a lot can happen in the interim. He is happy to hold but wants to see production reach and sustain nameplate capacity before turning more positive.
quote: With Karoon energy, I think first of all, single asset, still finding its way in ramp up period. Yes, the free cash flow, if you look at the free cash flow for Karoon energy, FY28 looks like it's going to start to look very attractive, but a lot can happen in between that. But the other final point is, I think as you noted, Nadine, these are stocks which are very much closely correlated with obviously the headline commodity. This is even more because of its pure play and single asset. So, I'd be a neutral on it. Again, I really need to see production wrap up to nameplate capacity and then delivering on an ongoing basis. But happy to hold it in the interim.

headline: Riesz bullish on outdoor advertising sector as advertising executives report strong and growing demand
reasoning: Recent conversations with advertising executives confirm that outdoor media is where significant demand is concentrating. This structural shift validates the investment case for oOh!media and explains why Nine Network has also made a play in the space. The positive demand outlook underpins the sector's valuation even in a softer macro environment.
quote: The outdoor media space, which obviously nine network has also made a plane, is the space you want to be. In the last couple of weeks, I was talking to a few advertising execs. And again, outdoor media is where most of these guys are seeing a lot of demand for.

headline: Riesz flags Strait of Hormuz disruptions as underappreciated supply chain and inflation risk heading into reporting season
reasoning: The Strait of Hormuz has been repeatedly closed and reopened with minimal market consequences despite contributing 20-30% of global supply chain flows including oil, energy and agriculture. Riesz sees this as a persistent macro risk and intends to focus on what companies are seeing in supply chain disruption alongside consumer demand signals during the upcoming reporting season.
quote: We've obviously seen Shredder Hormuz being closed again. I mean, it's become a bit of a joke. Apparently, this particular stretch of water contributes 30 odd percent, 20, 30 percent to global supply chains, oil, energy, agriculture, and the fact that we can flip it on and off without having any consequences. It's a bridge that we still are struggling to cross. So, yeah, this is something we will be focusing on. And more importantly, I think at the end of the day, when you look at the returns profile... investors more broadly, especially if you've been exposed to global equities, which have done much better even in AUD terms, you wouldn't be complaining too much.

headline: Riesz sells Kogan.com citing lack of quality, management credibility issues and no identifiable moat
reasoning: Kogan's share price has mirrored its volatile EPS and margin history, and management liquidated a significant portion of their holdings near the top. The stock is trading on 22-23x PE for mid-single-digit revenue growth with uncertain margin improvement, leaving earnings growth looking lacklustre. There is no clear competitive moat beyond scale. Riesz would prefer Wesfarmers, JB Hi-Fi or Sigma/Chemist Warehouse over Kogan for retail exposure.
quote: You look at a share price chart, right? Going back the last five years, some of the comments that we made about management team, you know, look, just kind of doesn't pass the pub test. But you look at that chart right there, and you look at the EPS and margins, they pretty much have gone up and down exactly like that... trading on 23, 22 times P, multiple, giving you a single-digit, mid-single-digit revenue growth. Now, if the margin improvement doesn't come in over the same period, you're looking at a pretty lacklustre earnings growth as well off the back of that. And nothing really, I don't know where the moat is besides potentially scale, perhaps. So I would avoid. I think there are better retailers out there. You know, you're West farmers of the world, you're JB Hi-Fis of the world. You look at, you know, even the Sigma Farms, pseudo-coloured guys... I think you can back good business models you can back. So for me, it's a sell.

headline: Riesz would trim oOh!media profits with three PE bids on the table but sees residual value to $1.80-$2.00
reasoning: Riesz's firm has been positive on oOh!media and owns it, having been bullish below $1 as it was too cheap given cyclical headwinds. Three private equity bidders have since emerged, validating the thesis. Valuation at $1.80-$2.00 depending on cycle, suggests the current $1.60-$1.65 price still offers a 10-20% discount to fair value. However, given the macro backdrop he recommends taking some profits, while holding the remainder pending deal completion.
quote: We have been positive on the stock. We have been sort of thumping the table on from a buy perspective. We own it as well anywhere below a dollar, even with all the cyclical headwinds was just way too cheap. Yeah, we got lucky from a bid perspective... I know I think you can get a valuation of $1.80 to $2 for Umedia, depending on what kind of cyclical environment we are in or trading environment we are in. I think at $1.60 to $1.65, I think whoever picks it up is still getting a margin of safety of probably 10%, 15% in terms of 10%, 20% in valuation terms. But given where the macro is for Australia, the overall global macro backdrop, I would be certainly taking some profits off the table here, but I would hold it.

headline: Riesz long-term positive on gold and expects further M&A consolidation among ASX gold producers
reasoning: Riesz and his firm remain long-term positive on gold and the equities leveraged to it. He expects ongoing corporate activity as mergers and scale acquisitions are often more efficient than organic exploration-to-production pathways. The firm's primary exposures are Northern Star and Evolution Mining rather than mid-tier names like Genesis Minerals.
quote: I think the whole Gold space, even Gold today, was sold off because the hostilities in Iran have kicked off again. But I think we're still long-term positive on Gold. And so the equities that are leveraged to that will do well. Similar to Genesis, I think you'll see more and more corporate activity within this space, especially when it's sometimes, a lot of times, makes a lot more sense to acquire or merge to get that scale benefits and then divest underperforming assets rather than organically take particular assets through exploration to production.

headline: Zach Riaz prefers Ampol over Viva Energy in the fuel retail space, citing stronger returns and balance sheet.
reasoning: Banyan Tree has been recommending Ampol as the preferred exposure in the fuel retail and refining sector, contrasting it favourably to Viva Energy's high leverage and thin ROIC. No additional specific reasoning was provided beyond this relative preference.
quote: From our perspective, we prefer AMPL in this space, ALD, which is where we've been recommending investing in. But this for us, the debt level and the return on invested capital level is a bit too skinny and too high.

headline: Zach Riaz is neutral on ASX, flagging valuation is not compelling but sees a trading opportunity below $50 pending new CEO clarity.
reasoning: Zach acknowledges ASX has high-quality monopoly characteristics with strong margins, but says the valuation is not cheap enough to justify a strong conviction buy. He notes the recent ASIC settlement removes one headwind and believes the stock can find a floor, but a lot depends on what the incoming CEO does with the cost base and investment profile. He suggests a swing trade below $50-45 for traders but is not a fundamental buyer. At roughly 20x forward earnings and a 3.7% yield, he sees it as fairly valued relative to global peers.
quote: Yeah, it looks interesting, but it's hard to get any more positive. You've got a new CEO still to come. Look, on key metrics, it's a high quality business. You know, I think Jonathan does describe it appropriately. It's a lazy monopoly. But, you know, so it's got to have high margins and whatnot. And because of all those factors, I think it does find a flaw. I think anything below $50 or $45, I think you have a swing as a trader. But in terms of fundamental, is this going to be your only compound? I think you've got to get the new CEO come in. The recent ASIC settlement, you know, probably removes one sort of headwind.

headline: Zach Riaz is neutral on Greatland Gold, saying the recent outperformance has normalised its previously cheap relative valuation.
reasoning: Zach thinks GGP has high-quality assets, including former Newcrest mines, and likes the gold-copper mix. However, he notes the company is entering a large CAPEX cycle of $1-1.5bn and free cashflow monetisation is likely 1-2 years away. Banyan Tree took profits on gold earlier this year and rotated into a broader commodities basket which has outperformed. He expects gold to find a floor but whether it trends higher depends largely on Middle East developments. The recent rally, both absolute and relative, has made valuation look more neutral.
quote: With this particular company, T1 Asset, it is coming to again, that asset period, CAPEX cycle. I think it's meant to spend about 1 to $1.5 billion. Again, we like it when cashflow is increasing or your peak CAPEX, and then you're starting to just monetize the free cashflow. I think that's probably a year or two away for this company. Obviously, it's rallied, it's traded much better than some of its gold peers. And I think that's been, because it was also trading at a fairly and relatively attractive, multiple relative to the other guys. But I think the recent rally, both absolute and relative, means the valuation is looking a bit more neutral at these levels.

headline: Banyan Tree neutral on Metcash — holds it in dividend strategy when Coles/Woolworths PE too high, but sees hardware as standout and notes Aldi share gains as structural headwind.
reasoning: Riaz argues Metcash's wholesale model is structurally disadvantaged versus Coles/Woolworths vertically integrated model and Aldi's international scale. He estimates Aldi has taken 20-30% of his grocery basket, hurting IGA volumes. However, Metcash has executed a reasonable turnaround and the 6% dividend yield is attractive when the majors trade at elevated multiples. Trading update shows consumers returning in June after soft March/April. Hardware is described as the segment generating most interest.
quote: You've had Woolworths and Coles who control their own stores and therefore control their supply chains and therefore can compute on price. Metcash has a business where it is the wholesale provider. Two guys that run IGA. Those guys are sometimes one storeperson or they have multiple stores. So they've got to manage their costs. They can only do certain compute on certain pricing. And then you've got Audi that's coming to the business, international player that's got financial backing has taken, I would say, 20 to 30 percent of our grocery basket.

headline: Zach Riaz is neutral on Qantas, viewing it as a high-quality trading stock rather than a compounder, noting its strong jet fuel hedging.
reasoning: Zach does not see airlines as compounding businesses and would not hold Qantas over a five-year horizon as a core investment. However, he acknowledges the industry structure has improved with fewer irrational competitors. He notes Qantas is one of the most hedged airlines on jet fuel, meaning Asian airlines are more exposed to spot price volatility than Qantas is. Any geopolitical blowup will instantly derate the stock, making it better suited to active trading. He recommends managing position size actively.
quote: Look, we've never liked airlines as a compounding business. So the first question we ask, when we're looking at a stock, would we own the stock in the five years time? And what we really want that is a compounding effect and growth over that earnings and hopefully dividends at the same time. Qantas obviously is a good quality company. I would say the industry structure has changed a fair bit. It was a lot more irrational, you know, Virgin's gone in and out of administration. You know, Tiger Airways has come and gone. And I think we are at a juncture where the overall industry setup is a little bit better. In terms of the latest issues around, you know, airlines being sold on the back of fuel costs, well, Qantas is one of them highly hedged airlines. In fact, the Asian airlines are much more exposed to this movement in spot prices.

headline: Zach Riaz holds Lottery Corporation in his dividend strategy but sees limited top-line growth acceleration and a ceiling on valuation.
reasoning: Zach has held TLC in his dividend strategy for some time, valuing its low-beta defensive characteristics. He notes the lottery business is TLC's dominant EBIT driver but sees only low single-digit top-line growth potential despite management's ambitions for mid-single-digit growth. Digitalization and new products can enhance earnings growth beyond the revenue line, but the already-elevated P/E means there is a valuation ceiling. The yield is not particularly high either, making this a quality but not exciting defensive play.
quote: Look, it's a company we've liked for a very long time. It's in our dividend strategy. It's been there for a while, provides low beta as well. The defensive quality of its end markets. Obviously, its biggest revenue, sorry, EBIT driver is the lottery's business. But it is it is a low growth. There's you know, I know at the recent at the recent investor day, you know, management is looking to get that top line growth, you know, accelerated to more that single, mid single digit growth versus sort of low to low double low single digit growth. And but, you know, at the end of the day, I can't see this, you know, from a top line growth perspective, accelerating in a meaningful, meaningful way.

headline: Zach Riaz is neutral on Technology One, saying strong double-digit growth is priced in at 60x P/E and 30-32x EV/EBITDA.
reasoning: Zach acknowledges TNE's impressive growth profile—nearly 15% revenue CAGR and 22% earnings CAGR in their forecasts, with revenue reaching $1 billion ahead of schedule. However, he cannot get to a thumping buy because the current price above $30 requires 60x P/E and 30-32x EV/EBITDA, multiples he views as demanding given broader macro uncertainty. He sees it as a core holding and would look to add on price weakness, having missed the bargain entry at $20.
quote: The only tell that we recently run the numbers on this. And it is it's very hard to get across to a thumping bite on valuation grounds, right? You know, margin expansion, we've got it in our numbers, them achieving the one billion dollars of revenue line, we've got ahead one year ahead. We've got double digit earnings growth, revenue growth and top line growth, etc. We've got it. And so we've got a we've got an average K of nearly 15 percent per annum on revenue and nearly 22 percent per annum in terms of bottom line. So really growth numbers. Now, some may go. I will take this at any price. But, you know, to justify a price from a EBE bit, a multiple perspective and a P multiple perspective, you have to plug in at least around 60 times P number and you have to plug in about 30 to 32 times EBE number to get above 30 dollars, 33 dollars.

headline: Zach Riaz rates Vicinity Centres a buy for dividend investors, citing limited new retail supply and positive leasing spreads at quality centres.
reasoning: Zach holds Vicinity in his dividend strategy and is broadly positive on quality retail REITs. He highlights that new retail supply in Sydney and Melbourne has virtually stopped, growing at just 0.1-0.5% p.a. versus 2.5-2.7% historically. He notes people still want experiences and foot traffic at quality centres remains strong, with waiting lists for new tenants and positive lease spreads emerging. On valuation he is more neutral, but as a dividend play he rates it a buy.
quote: We really like retail space. And to be honest, we really like we put central group in the same same bucket. It has obviously been on a trading range, as you can see on your chart. But the supply of new retail coming quality retail is limited. So, you know, I was looking at a statistic, Sydney and Melbourne supply over the last sort of from 2010 to 2019 has grown at a Kego of about two and a half to two point seven percent per annum. The next sort of five, six, seven years is basically growing point one to point five percent. So there's no new supply coming on. And this whole narrative around that everyone shot from home absolutely not go to your centers on the weekend. People are out there. People want experiences.

headline: Zach Riaz avoids Viva Energy, flagging thin returns on invested capital, 4.5x net debt/EBITDA and preference for Ampol instead.
reasoning: Zach argues Viva's return on invested capital barely covers its cost of capital, meaning volatile refining margins can quickly swing earnings into negative territory against covenants. Net debt at 4.5x EBITDA is dangerously high. He prefers ALD (Ampol) in the fuel retail and refining space, where returns are healthier and balance sheet risk is lower. He notes his DCF from the time of Viva's IPO valued the stock at around $2.40-$2.50, consistent with where it currently trades, suggesting limited upside.
quote: The return on invested capital is pretty low. It's pretty close to where its cost of capital is. And then if you get any sort of movement around in refining margins, that can move the delta very quickly on that. And we think quality companies should be earning wall above their cost of capital. And I think that then invariably gets reflected in your share price over the longterm and therefore return. So that's one part. The other big part about this company is net debt is very high, 4.5 times. And that's net debt to EBITDA. You start getting the EBITDA earnings line moving around, that debt structure or those covenants certainly start to become in question. So a void or what do you think? It's a void for us. Do not want to be around leveraged planes.

headline: Zach Riaz holds a small Wisetech position hoping for a private equity takeout, calling the situation an 'absolute shambles'.
reasoning: Zach agrees the company has a great product but the governance situation has become a case study in mismanagement. He sees two paths to resolution: Richard White exits voluntarily, or uses his 34% stake to take the company private. He notes early institutional shareholders who backed White at $70-90 have now seen the stock hit five-year lows. His small holding is predicated on the hope that private equity arrives to take it out, given the workforce reduction already underway resembles a PE playbook.
quote: It's a great company, great product, and it's become an absolute shambles case studies for MBA classes around the world, frankly. And I agree with Jonathan, either the founder needs to leave or he can use this 34 percent shareholding and take this private. Do whatever you want to do as a private company then. But, you know, it's interesting. There was a lot of shareholders when, you know, where there's fire, whether it's smoke, there's fire. And when this this whole notion originally started, a lot of the big shareholders said, no, we want him to stay. That was about seventy, ninety dollars. What it was. Well, congratulations. This is where we're at now. So I think the best outcome for existing investors is private equity comes and takes this out.

headline: Zach Riaz is neutral on Advanced Energy Minerals, citing execution risk, funding risk and illiquidity typical of early-stage miners.
reasoning: Zach had not previously heard of AEM and acknowledges it falls outside his normal screens. He flags three key risks for early-stage producers: execution risk on production ramp-up, potential funding risk, and commodity/market price risk. He notes that even well-managed companies with quality assets can struggle through ramp-up phases, and liquidity constraints make it difficult for larger investors to get comfortable.
quote: Generally I get production and ramp up of, you know, revenue with these kinds of names normally comes with execution risk, potential funding risk. And then there's the commodity and market risk added to that. And so from our perspective, these are ones that unless you really have some deep insight into the stock, the company management teams, we've seen some really good companies with very strong management teams and assets and their ramp up. And they're not obviously as liquid or small as this and they still run into trouble.

headline: Banyan Tree rotated from gold to broader commodities basket earlier this year, seeing gold-risk correlation as a concern but now approaching a floor.
